entries.claim: With the true initial contact s_0 given, adding the explicit R2 output loss to the deterministic dense generator (D1 versus D0) did not improve it. TACO: participation, centroid, normal and wrench-profile errors are 1.8-5.4 % higher and the dense error 1.4 % higher (all intervals exclude zero). ARCTIC: centroid, normal and wrench-profile errors are 3.1-4.9 % higher (intervals exclude zero), while participation (+0.8 % [-2.1, +3.4]) and dense error (+0.7 % [-0.7, +2.0]) are not distinguishable from no change. Of the six reported errors only the contact amount is lower, by under 1 % (TACO -0.9 % [-1.4, -0.4]; ARCTIC -0.8 % [-1.8, +0.3], interval includes zero). This holds for the one surrogate tested (differentiable grid R2 operator, weights 0.3 / 1 / 3, validation chose 0.3).

Metrics: participation Hamming (fraction of 6 hand parts wrong), centroid distance (object lengths), normal angle (deg), wrench-profile relative L1 (proxy for functional grasp capability), amount L1, dense error E_C.

The structural metrics are extracted from a generated map with the ground-truth hand-part label of each surface point (evaluate.py line 68), so they measure whether contact appears where the real hand's parts are, not whether the model identifies fingers.

On parts active in both the generated and the real map the centroid error of D1 is nominally lower: -3.47 % [-7.87, +0.43] (TACO), -0.53 % [-3.28, +2.88] (ARCTIC) (metric centroid_both); the reported centroid metric mixes participation and location errors.
decision_summary.csv labels the TACO deterministic case 'marginal (< 5 %)': that is a rule output (a metric counts as worse only at +5 % or more), not a marginal gain.
Models were selected by early stopping (all runs stopped by patience), not trained to a step cap (run_config.csv).
entries.claim_as_extracted: With the true initial contact s_0 given, adding the explicit R2 output loss to the deterministic dense generator (D1 versus D0) did not improve it: on TACO the participation, centroid, normal and wrench-profile errors are 1.8-5.4 % higher with intervals that exclude zero; on ARCTIC centroid, normal and wrench-profile errors are 3.1-4.9 % higher (intervals exclude zero) while participation is not distinguishable from no change; only the contact-amount error improves, by under 1 %.
entries.correction_reason: All numbers and directions are confirmed in paired_comparisons.csv. Two small imprecisions: 'only the amount improves' is stated without saying that on ARCTIC the amount interval includes zero and the sign differs between seeds (it is only in the caveats), and the claim omits the dense error (worse on TACO, tie on ARCTIC). Scope ('this surrogate under this recipe', report section 16) should travel with the claim.

entries.claim_as_extracted: Context for reading the comparison: with the true s_0 the dense-only deterministic generator D0 already recovers much of the R2-level structure relative to holding s_0 (participation error 0.182 against 0.477 on TACO, 0.192 against 0.339 on ARCTIC), and with sampled s_0 the end-to-end error is dominated by the sampled initial contact (D0 dense error 2.525 / 3.464 against 1.775 / 1.963 with the true s_0).
entries.correction_reason: Values confirmed. 'Recovers much of the structure' is an interpretation; the numbers with the floor say it directly. The protocol-A and protocol-B dense errors cover different frame ranges (B includes frame 0), so the comparison is not like-for-like, and 'dominated by the sampled s_0' is the report's reading (report section 8), which should be attributed.

dataset_differences: Output R2 loss, deterministic (D1 vs D0): on TACO every interval excludes zero (participation +3.5 %, centroid +5.4 %, normal +2.2 %, wrench +1.8 %, dense +1.4 %); on ARCTIC participation (+0.8 % [-2.1, +3.4]), dense error (+0.7 % [-0.7, +2.0]) and amount (-0.8 % [-1.8, +0.3]) are not distinguishable from no change, while centroid (+4.9 %), normal (+3.9 %) and wrench (+3.1 %) are.

Hidden head, deterministic (D2 vs D1): TACO worse on all of dense / participation / centroid / normal / wrench with intervals clear of zero; ARCTIC only centroid (+6.5 %) and normal (+6.4 %) are distinguishable. The frame-to-frame change drops by 3.8 % on TACO but 28.0 % on ARCTIC.

Output R2 loss, diffusion (S1 vs S0): dense error +6.8 % on TACO, -0.0 % on ARCTIC; amount error -1.0 % on TACO, -6.8 % on ARCTIC; participation +8.5 % (TACO, interval excludes zero) vs +2.7 % [-2.0, +7.9] (ARCTIC).

Diffusion vs deterministic with the true s_0 (S0 vs D0): dense error +14.8 % on TACO, +26.6 % on ARCTIC; amount error +4.7 % vs +20.9 %; wrench-profile error +1.0 % [-0.3, +2.2] on TACO (tie) vs +2.7 % [+0.1, +5.1] on ARCTIC (slightly worse).

Temporal jitter: diffusion samples change about 3.6-6.9 times as much per frame as real TACO trajectories (S0 1.148, S2 2.169 vs GT 0.315) and about 9.8-17.2 times as much on ARCTIC (S0 1.586, S2 2.769 vs GT 0.161). The deterministic D0 changes about half as much as real data on TACO (0.160 vs 0.315) and nearly as much on ARCTIC (0.144 vs 0.161).

Diversity levels are larger on ARCTIC in absolute terms (future-only D_Z 1.152 vs 0.817; initial-only 2.483 vs 1.628), with a similar future / initial ratio (stored 0.47 ARCTIC, 0.51 TACO). Holding the sampled s_0 gives more R2 spread than evolving it on TACO (2.374 vs 1.628) but less on ARCTIC (1.754 vs 2.483).

Dense predictability: with the true s_0, D0 halves the dense error of holding s_0 on TACO (1.775 vs 3.539) but improves it only slightly on ARCTIC (1.963 vs 2.242); with sampled s_0 the ARCTIC dense error of the evolved trajectory (3.464) is no lower than holding the sample (3.455), TACO 2.525 vs 4.164.

With sampled s_0 (protocol B) the diffusion model is slightly better than the deterministic one on structure on ARCTIC (S0 vs D0 participation -5.1 % [-8.0, -1.8], wrench -2.7 % [-4.7, -0.6]) and slightly worse on TACO (participation +2.4 % [+0.3, +4.4]); dense error is about +11 % on both.

S2 (diffusion + output loss + hidden head) is nominally better than D0 on ARCTIC structure (participation 0.175 vs 0.192, centroid 0.286 vs 0.299, normal 47.3 vs 48.9 deg) and equal on TACO (0.181 vs 0.182), at a much higher dense error (2.931 vs 1.963 ARCTIC; 2.494 vs 1.775 TACO); no paired test of this pair exists.
Sample size: TACO 364 test sequences from 186 takes; ARCTIC 186 test sequences from 44 takes, so ARCTIC intervals are several times wider.
Extraction floor differs: participation 0.102 (TACO) vs 0.047 (ARCTIC); wrench 0.372 vs 0.326.
OakInk2 is not part of this experiment (excluded in report section 4); every statement of this block is for TACO and ARCTIC only.
do_not_claim: Structural (R2) supervision cannot help, or R2 is the wrong structure: only one surrogate (a differentiable grid R2 operator with ground-truth part labels), weights 0.3 / 1 / 3 and one training recipe were tested; nothing between 0 and 0.3. The report's wording is 'this surrogate under this recipe does not help'.

R2 supervision significantly hurts every metric on both datasets: on ARCTIC participation, dense error and amount are not distinguishable from no change, and the amount error improves slightly on TACO.
The output loss gave a 'marginal gain' on TACO (the decision table's 'marginal (< 5 %)' is a rule label; the significant changes are all for the worse except the amount, -0.9 %).
The hidden head makes D2 significantly worse than D0: no paired D2-versus-D0 comparison exists; the claim rests on D2 vs D1 plus D1 vs D0.
Diffusion is worse on structure: at the dense-only level it ties (intervals include zero), and at the hidden-head level one S2 sample is better than D2 on participation / centroid / normal.
'S models are 15-26 % worse on dense error': true for S0 and S1 against their matched deterministic model (14.8-26.6 %), not for S2 vs D2 (+31.8 % TACO, +46.9 % ARCTIC).
'3.7-17x the real frame-to-frame change' as one range: it pools TACO (3.6-6.9x) with ARCTIC (9.8-17.2x) and S0 with S2.

Human futures given s_0 are deterministic or unimodal, or 'universally deterministic': only one future is observed per condition and the tested diffusion recipe is noisy; the supported statement is that this stochastic future model gave no K = 1 structural benefit.

Future stochasticity is unnecessary in general, or 'initial stochasticity is sufficient' as an established fact: 'Case A' is a rule output of aggregate.decision(), which has no branch for a standalone Case C; the report's wording is 'Case A, with a Case-C caveat for this diffusion recipe'.

Best-of-10 gains show that the diffusion captures alternative valid futures: best-of-10 is an oracle against the single observed future, and even then the dense error stays 7.4 % (TACO) / 16.6 % (ARCTIC) worse.

The 2-5x diversity multiplier is a like-for-like decomposition, or 'R2 and wrench diversity are 5x larger': the two sides use different protocols and frame ranges, the multipliers exist only in prose, D_Z and wrench are 2.0-3.2x, and the 5x end is the centroid component.

The initial sampler's diversity is 'meaningful' in the sense of covering real alternative grasps: diversity is a spread, the sampled s_0 are far from the true s_0 (error 2.35 TACO / 2.40 ARCTIC), and no coverage test was run.
The deterministic model reproduces real temporal dynamics: it changes less from frame to frame than the real data (about half on TACO).
D0 is the best model on every metric: it has the lowest dense error on both datasets, but S2 is nominally at or below it on ARCTIC structural metrics.
The generators know which finger touches: structural metrics are extracted with ground-truth hand-part labels; no model outputs finger identity.
This experiment shows that R2 is a useful analysis / relational representation: that comes from the earlier structure / variance study; here R2 was only a training-time loss and an evaluation lens.

The jitter is a sampler or implementation bug, or conversely an inherent property of diffusion: the diagnostic (one seed per dataset, 96 sequences) only shows it does not depend on the number of DDIM steps for this trained model.

End-to-end generation is solved by 'sample s_0, then evolve deterministically': with sampled s_0 the error is dominated by the sampled initial contact, and on ARCTIC the evolved dense error is no lower than holding the sample.
The models were trained to convergence, or the hypotheses were pre-registered: every run stopped by early-stopping patience, and the report does not use the word pre-registered.

Wrench results as statements about human intent, or any robot null-space reading: the wrench profile is a modelled proxy for functional grasp capability (one unit-force friction-cone patch per active hand part).
Any OakInk2 statement for this block, or any number pooled or averaged over TACO and ARCTIC.
